title: Monitoring with Prometheus
intro: Part 8 left hello-devops running on kind, deployed by Argo CD. This part teaches you to see how it is doing. Day 41 builds the ideas every monitoring tool shares: signals, SLOs, error budgets and alerts on what users feel. Days 42 to 44 put them to work with Prometheus: a Compose lab on your laptop, PromQL from the first query to a full RED view, alerts that reach a receiver, and finally the same setup on Kubernetes.

lessons.goal: By the end you can explain the four signals, describe a service with RED and a machine with USE, turn an SLO into an error budget and burn rates, and say which alerts deserve a page.

sections.h: Monitoring and observability
sections.body:
Monitoring means you decide in advance what can go wrong, measure it, and get told when it happens. Is hello-devops answering? Is the disk filling up? Each of those is a check someone wrote on purpose.

**Observability** is how well you can answer a question you did not plan for, using the data the system already gives off. Here is one: why did requests from the mobile app get slow at 14:00, but only for users with items in their basket? No alert you wrote last month answers that. If your data has enough detail, you can still find the answer without shipping new code.

You need both. Monitoring catches the problems you know about and wakes someone up. Observability helps that person find out why. Google's [SRE book chapter on monitoring](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) adds one more split worth knowing:
- White-box monitoring looks inside: numbers and logs the app reports about itself.
- Black-box monitoring looks from outside, like a user would: does the page load at all?

White-box data explains a problem. Black-box checks catch the problems your app cannot see, such as a broken DNS record in front of it.

sections.h: Four signals, four questions
sections.body:
The data a system gives off about itself is called telemetry. It comes in four kinds, usually called signals:
- Metrics: numbers over time, like requests per second. They tell you that something is wrong.
- Logs: one line of text per event, with a timestamp. They tell you what happened to one request.
- Traces: one request followed through every service, split into timed steps called spans. They tell you where the time or the error came from.
- Profiles: which functions use the CPU and memory. They tell you which code is expensive.

Metrics are cheap because they are already summed up. A thousand requests a second become one counter that Prometheus reads every 15 seconds. Logs and traces grow with traffic, so teams keep less of them, or only a sample.

A real incident often uses them in that order. A metric alert fires: 3% of checkouts fail. A trace of one failed checkout shows a 5-second wait on the payment service. That service's logs for the same trace ID say its database connection pool was full.

The next parts of the course follow the same split:
- Part 9 (Days 41 to 44): metrics and alerts with Prometheus.
- Part 10 (Days 45 and 46): dashboards with Grafana, and logs with Loki.
- Part 11 (Days 47 to 49): logs with the Elastic stack, traces with OpenTelemetry.
- Part 12 (Days 50 and 51): Dynatrace, one commercial product that collects every signal.

sections.h: Golden signals, RED and USE
sections.body:
Which few numbers should you watch first? Three well-known checklists answer that, and they overlap a lot.

The four golden signals come from the SRE book: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Its advice is blunt: if you can only measure four metrics of a user-facing system, measure these.

The [RED method](https://grafana.com/blog/the-red-method-how-to-instrument-your-services/), from Tom Wilkie, keeps three of them for anything that serves requests:
- Rate: requests per second.
- Errors: failed requests per second, or the share that fail.
- Duration: how long requests take, usually as percentiles.

A percentile reads like this: a p95 of 200 ms means 95% of requests took 200 ms or less. Averages hide the slow ones, so teams watch p95 or p99.

The [USE method](https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html), from Brendan Gregg, is for resources such as CPU, memory, disks and network cards:
- Utilization: how busy the resource was, such as CPU busy 70% of the time.
- Saturation: extra work waiting because the resource is full, such as a queue of runnable processes.
- Errors: error events, such as failed disk reads.

Grafana's dashboard guide says it well: USE tells you how happy your machines are, RED tells you how happy your users are. For hello-devops, RED is requests per second to `/`, the share of 5xx answers, and the p95 response time. You will write all three in PromQL on Day 43.

sections.h: SLIs, SLOs and SLAs
sections.body:
An SLI (service level indicator) says how good the service is, seen from the user's side. The most useful shape is a ratio of good events to valid events:
- Availability SLI: responses that are not 5xx, divided by all responses.
- Latency SLI: responses faster than 300 ms, divided by all responses.

An SLO (service level objective) is a target for an SLI over a time window. For example: 99.9% of requests to `/` succeed, measured over the last 30 days. An SLA (service level agreement) is a contract with a customer that says what happens when you miss, often money back. Teams set the SLA looser than the SLO, so they notice trouble before it costs money.

Do not aim for 100%. The SRE book's chapter on [embracing risk](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/) gives the reason: a user on a phone that works 99% of the time cannot tell 99.99% from 99.999%. Each extra nine costs far more work, and users never notice it. So pick a target that keeps users happy and treat it as a floor and a ceiling. If you are far more reliable than your SLO, you are probably shipping slower than you could.

sections.h: Error budgets and burn rate
sections.body:
The error budget is the failure the SLO allows: 100% minus the SLO. For 99.9% that is 0.1%. With 200,000 requests a day, 30 days hold 6,000,000 requests, and 6,000 of them may fail. If everything fails at once, 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes of full outage.

The budget turns an argument into arithmetic. Developers want to ship, operators want quiet nights, and both can look at the same number. While budget is left, you ship at normal speed and take some risks. When it is spent, the SRE book's answer is to pause risky releases until reliability is back.

The burn rate says how fast you are spending it: the current error ratio divided by the budget. With a 0.1% budget:
- 0.1% of requests failing is burn rate 1. The budget lasts exactly 30 days.
- 0.6% failing is burn rate 6. The budget is gone in 5 days.
- 1.44% failing is burn rate 14.4. The budget is gone in about 2 days, and one hour of this spends 2% of it.

Those numbers come from Google's [SRE Workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/): page at 14.4 over one hour or 6 over six hours, and open a ticket at 1 over three days. Day 44 turns them into Prometheus alerts. Burn rate works better than a raw error count because it already knows your traffic and your target.

sections.h: Alert on symptoms, and keep pages rare
sections.body:
A page is an alert that interrupts a person, maybe at 3 a.m. Each one costs sleep and focus, so every page must be urgent, real and something a human can act on. The [Prometheus alerting guide](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/alerting/) puts it in one line: keep alerting simple, alert on symptoms, and avoid pages where there is nothing to do.

A symptom is something users feel: errors, slow answers, the site down. A cause is a reason that might lead to a symptom: high CPU, a busy disk, a pod restart. Causes are useful on dashboards, where you look during an investigation. They make poor pages, because many of them never hurt anyone. A server at 90% CPU that answers every request in 50 ms is simply doing its job.

Sort every alert into one of three groups:
- Page: users hurt now and a human must act now. A fast error budget burn, or the service down.
- Ticket: needs a human in working hours. A slow burn, or a certificate that expires in 10 days.
- Dashboard only: everything else, such as CPU, memory and single restarts.

Too many alerts cause alert fatigue: people learn that pages are usually noise and start to ignore them, including the real one. If an alert fires and nobody needs to do anything, delete it or make it a ticket.

sections.h: On-call and blameless postmortems
sections.body:
On-call means one person carries the pager for a shift, often a week, and answers pages within minutes. Teams keep it bearable with three habits:
- Few pages, each one tied to a symptom.
- A runbook for every alert: a short page with what the alert means and the first things to check.
- A second person to call when the first one is stuck.

After an incident, the team writes a postmortem: what happened, the timeline, the impact on users, and what will stop it from happening again. Blameless means the document looks for gaps in systems and processes, not for a person to punish. If one command could take production down, the fix is a safer command; blaming the engineer only teaches everyone to hide mistakes. Google's [postmortem chapter](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) describes the practice in detail.

The SLO links all of this. It defines what working means, the burn rate decides when someone gets paged, and the postmortem decides what to change so next month's budget lasts longer.

lessons.analogy: Think of a train company that promises 99% of its trains arrive within five minutes of the timetable each month. That promise is the SLO, and the 1% of trains allowed to be late is the error budget. If the company has used little of it by mid-month, it can close a track for repairs; if a storm has used it all, repairs wait. Where it breaks: trains run on a fixed timetable, while software failures come in sudden bursts, which is why you watch the burn rate and not only the monthly total.

worked.title: An SLO for hello-devops, from numbers to an alert plan

steps.say: Start with what users do. hello-devops has one real job: the JSON at `/`. A good event is a response that is not 5xx. A valid event is any response to `/`. A 404 for a mistyped URL is the user's mistake, so it does not count against you.
Pick a target and a window, then let the Day 41 script do the arithmetic. I guessed 200,000 requests a day.
steps.code:
$ python3 observability/error_budget.py 99.9 30 200000
SLO 99.90% over 30 days
Error budget: 0.10% of requests
Full outage allowed: 43.2 minutes
Failed requests allowed: 6,000 of 6,000,000
Burn rate 14.4: error ratio 1.44%, budget gone in 2.1 days; 1 h of this uses 2% (page)
Burn rate    6: error ratio 0.60%, budget gone in 5.0 days; 6 h of this uses 5% (page)
Burn rate    1: error ratio 0.10%, budget gone in 30.0 days; 72 h of this uses 10% (ticket)

steps.say: Read it like a budget. One bad deploy that breaks everything for 20 minutes spends almost half the month. That tells you something concrete: a rollback must take minutes, not an hour.

Now a bad hour: 2% of requests fail for 60 minutes. The burn rate is 0.02 / 0.001 = 20, above 14.4, so this should page. One hour at burn rate 20 spends 20/720 of the budget, because 30 days have 720 hours.
Compare a slow leak: 0.3% of requests fail all week. That is burn rate 3, and the budget lasts 10 days. Nobody needs to wake up, but someone must fix it this week, so it is a ticket.
Write the plan down in plain words before any PromQL. Day 44 turns exactly these lines into `alerts.yml`. Each long window has a short partner, so the alert stops soon after the errors stop.
steps.code:
SLI:    responses to / that are not 5xx, divided by all responses to /
SLO:    99.9% over 30 days  (error budget 0.1%)
Page:   error ratio > 1.44% over 1 h AND over 5 m
        or > 0.6% over 6 h AND over 30 m
Ticket: error ratio > 0.1% over 3 days AND over 6 h
Never page on: CPU, memory, single pod restarts (dashboard only)

code.title: observability/error_budget.py
code.src:
"""Turn an SLO into an error budget and burn rates (Day 41).

Usage:   python3 error_budget.py SLO_PERCENT [DAYS] [REQUESTS_PER_DAY]
Example: python3 error_budget.py 99.9 30 200000
"""

import sys

slo = float(sys.argv[1]) / 100  # 99.9 -> 0.999
days = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 30
per_day = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 0

budget = 1 - slo  # the share of requests that may fail
minutes = days * 24 * 60

print(f"SLO {slo:.2%} over {days:g} days")
print(f"Error budget: {budget:.2%} of requests")
print(f"Full outage allowed: {budget * minutes:.1f} minutes")
if per_day:
    total = per_day * days
    print(f"Failed requests allowed: {budget * total:,.0f} of {total:,.0f}")

# Burn rate = how fast you spend the budget. 1 means "used up exactly at the end".
# The three rows are the starting points from Google's SRE Workbook (Day 44):
# page at 14.4 over 1 hour or 6 over 6 hours, open a ticket at 1 over 3 days.
for burn, window_h, action in [(14.4, 1, "page"), (6, 6, "page"), (1, 72, "ticket")]:
    used = burn * window_h / (days * 24)
    print(
        f"Burn rate {burn:>4}: error ratio {burn * budget:.2%}, budget gone in {days / burn:.1f} days;"
        f" {window_h} h of this uses {used:.0%} ({action})"
    )

lessons.mistake: Paging on causes such as CPU above 80%, memory above 90% or any pod restart. These fire all the time without users noticing, so people stop trusting the pager. Page on symptoms (error budget burn, the service not answering) and put causes on a dashboard you open once a page fires.
lessons.real_world: At a payments company with a product called PayFlow, the card team might set an SLO of 99.95% of authorisations answered without error within 2 seconds, over 28 days. The on-call engineer is paged only on a fast burn of that budget. When the budget runs out, the team's written policy freezes feature releases until two weeks of clean numbers come back.

task.title: Measure an SLI by hand, then sort the alerts
steps: In your repo root, start the Day 15 stack with `docker compose up -d` and check that `curl localhost:8000/` answers.
Send 200 requests to `/` and save the status code and time of each one to `sli.txt`, using curl's `-w` option from Day 9.
Stop Redis with `docker compose stop redis`, then append 20 more requests to the same file. Each one takes a few seconds, because the app retries Redis before it gives up.
With awk (Day 5), count the good responses (status below 500) and print the availability SLI as a percentage. Then compute a latency SLI: the share that took 0.1 seconds or less.
Start Redis again. Run `error_budget.py` for a 99.5% SLO over 30 days with your own guess of daily traffic.
Work out the burn rate your measured error ratio means against that 99.5% SLO, and how many days the budget would last at that rate.

Sort these eight alerts into page, ticket or dashboard, with one line of why for each: CPU above 80% for 10 minutes; 5% of requests to `/` fail for 10 minutes; p95 latency above 2 seconds for 15 minutes; disk 70% full; a pod restarted once; a TLS certificate expires in 10 days; burn rate 1.5 over 3 days; no successful request at all for 2 minutes.
hints: `awk '$1 < 500' sli.txt | wc -l` counts the good lines, and `wc -l < sli.txt` counts all of them.
Burn rate is the error ratio divided by the budget. For 99.5% the budget is 0.5%, so 5% errors is burn rate 10.
For each alert, ask two questions: do users feel it now, and can a person fix it now?
task.done_when: You have an availability SLI from your own requests (mine was 200 good of 220, 90.91%), its burn rate against a 99.5% SLO, and all eight alerts sorted with a reason.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a product manager, in 3 to 4 sentences, what an error budget is and why it can let the team ship more, not less. Mention the SLO, the burn rate and what happens when the budget runs out.
explain_back.answer: Our SLO says 99.9% of requests must succeed over 30 days, so 0.1% may fail, and that 0.1% is our error budget. While budget is left we can ship features and take some risk, because a few failures are already priced in. The burn rate tells us how fast we are spending it: a fast burn pages someone, a slow burn becomes a ticket. If the budget runs out, we pause risky releases and fix reliability first, so we argue about a number instead of about feelings.

recap: Monitoring checks for known problems; observability lets you ask new questions of your telemetry.
Metrics say that something is wrong, traces say where, logs say what happened, profiles say which code is expensive.
RED (rate, errors, duration) describes a service from the user's side; USE (utilization, saturation, errors) describes a machine.
An SLI is good events over valid events, an SLO is its target over a window, and the error budget is 100% minus the SLO.
Burn rate is the error ratio divided by the budget: page on fast burns (14.4 over 1 hour, 6 over 6 hours), open a ticket on slow ones.
Page only on symptoms with a clear action, and learn from incidents with blameless postmortems.

check.q: An image-resize service gets 1,000,000 requests a month and has an SLO of 99.95%. How many failed requests does its monthly error budget allow?

check.q: Which of these is a saturation signal for a Postgres database server?
options: Queries per second
The share of queries that return an error
Queries waiting for a free connection
The median query time

check.q: Your SLO is 99.9%. For the last 6 hours 0.7% of requests failed, and the last 30 minutes look the same. What should happen?

Nothing: 99.3% success still sounds high
Add it to next quarter's planning notes
Restart every pod to clear the errors

interview.q: What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA?
interview.a: An SLI measures service quality from the user's point of view, usually good events divided by valid events, such as the share of requests that succeed. An SLO is the target for that SLI over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with customers that says what happens, often credits, if a promised level is missed. Teams set the SLO tighter than the SLA so they react before they owe anyone money.

interview.q: Why should alerts fire on symptoms rather than causes?
interview.a: Users feel symptoms such as errors and slow responses, so a symptom alert always means real pain. A cause such as high CPU may or may not hurt anyone, and there are far too many possible causes to alert on each one. Paging on causes produces false alarms, which trains people to ignore the pager. Causes still matter: they belong on dashboards, where the on-call engineer looks once a symptom alert fires.

interview.q: How would you choose an SLO for a new service?
interview.a: I would start with a simple SLI, such as successful requests over all requests, and measure what the service achieves today. Then I would pick a target a little below that, so the team is not paged from day one, and agree with the product owner what happens when the budget runs out. I would review it every quarter: if users complain while the SLO is met, the SLI or the target is wrong. I would never pick 100%, because it leaves no room for deploys and costs far more than users can notice.

deeper.body:
Why do the SLO alerts in this course compare two windows? Try the simple version first and see where it fails.

Alert 1 is a plain threshold: page when the error ratio over the last 5 minutes is above 0.1%. It fires on every small blip, such as ten bad requests during a deploy, and spends your nights on errors that barely touch the budget. Alert 2 uses a long window instead: page when the ratio over 30 days is above 0.1%. Now it fires far too late, and once it fires it stays on for days after the problem is fixed.

Burn rate fixes the size question. Paging at burn rate 14.4 over one hour means you only page when one hour has already spent 2% of the month's budget. A ten-request blip never gets there. A real outage gets there within minutes, because a total outage is a burn rate of 1,000 for a 99.9% SLO.

The short window fixes the reset question. A one-hour window remembers a bad spike for an hour, so the alert would keep firing long after you fixed it. The [SRE Workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/) adds a second condition with a window one twelfth as long, 5 minutes for the 1-hour alert. Both windows must be over the line. The 5-minute window drops back within minutes of the fix, so the page clears quickly too.

The Workbook then layers three pairs:
- Page: burn rate 14.4 over 1 hour and 5 minutes (2% of the budget).
- Page: burn rate 6 over 6 hours and 30 minutes (5% of the budget).
- Ticket: burn rate 1 over 3 days and 6 hours (10% of the budget).

These are starting numbers, and the Workbook says to tune them for your service. Day 44 turns them into Prometheus rules for hello-devops, with a `promtool` test that proves a slow leak opens a ticket but does not page.

One more thing to try on paper: a latency SLO. Write it as a ratio too, for example requests answered within 300 ms divided by all requests. Then the same budget and burn-rate maths works unchanged. This is why many teams prefer ratio SLIs over a rule like p99 below 300 ms: ratios add up across time and across servers, and percentiles do not.

lessons.title: Prometheus: architecture and the data model
lessons.goal: By the end you can run Prometheus next to hello-devops with Docker Compose, read a /metrics page line by line, explain what a time series is, pick the right metric type, and spot a label that would explode the number of series.

guess.q: hello-devops crashes and stops answering. How does Prometheus find out?
options: The app sends a last message to Prometheus before it dies
Its next scrape of the app fails, and it records up = 0
It does not notice; the graph just stays flat
Docker tells Prometheus that the container stopped
guess.why: Prometheus pulls. Every scrape records an `up` value for the target: 1 if the scrape worked, 0 if it failed. A dead app cannot push anything.

One HTTP GET of a target's /metrics page, done again every scrape interval.

sections.h: Prometheus pulls
sections.body:
Prometheus is a server that collects numbers from your programs every few seconds and stores them with a timestamp. It does this by pulling. Your app shows its current numbers on a plain web page, `/metrics`, and Prometheus fetches that page on a timer. One fetch is a scrape, and the thing it scrapes is a target.

Pulling sounds backwards if you know logging, where the app sends lines out. It has real advantages:
- Prometheus knows which targets should exist. If one does not answer, it records `up = 0` for it, a health check you get for free.
- You can read the same page yourself with `curl` while you debug.
- A slow or broken monitoring server never blocks your app. The app only keeps a few counters in memory.

Pushing still has a place. A batch job that runs for 20 seconds may finish before any scrape. For that case the docs describe the Pushgateway, and they say [it is usually only right](https://github.com/prometheus/docs/blob/main/docs/practices/pushing.md) for the result of service-level batch jobs. Prometheus 3 can also receive metrics pushed over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry protocol you meet on Day 49.

sections.h: The parts: server, targets, exporters
sections.body:
One Prometheus server is a single program with four jobs:
- A scraper that fetches every target each `scrape_interval` (default 1 minute; the lab uses 15 seconds).
- A time series database (TSDB) on local disk.
- A rule engine that runs recording rules (Day 43) and alerting rules (Day 44).
- A web UI and HTTP API that answer PromQL queries.

You list targets in `prometheus.yml` under `scrape_configs`. Each entry is a job: a group of targets that do the same work. The lab has four jobs: `prometheus` (it scrapes itself), `hello-devops`, `node` and `alertmanager`. In a big system you do not type addresses. Service discovery asks the platform for the current list instead: Kubernetes, Docker, AWS and plain files are all supported.

Many programs have no `/metrics` page. An exporter fills the gap: it reads numbers from the system and shows them in Prometheus format.
- [node_exporter](https://github.com/prometheus/node_exporter) shows CPU, memory, disk and network for a Linux machine, on port 9100.
- [blackbox_exporter](https://github.com/prometheus/blackbox_exporter) probes other services from outside (HTTP, TCP, DNS), on port 9115.

One warning for your Mac. Docker Desktop runs containers inside a small Linux virtual machine. So the node_exporter container in the lab reports that VM, not macOS. That is fine for learning PromQL; just do not read it as your laptop's numbers.

sections.h: Reading a /metrics page
sections.body:
Open `localhost:8000/metrics` and you see the exposition format: plain text, one sample per line. Here are the first lines for the app's own counter:
- `# HELP hello_requests_total Requests served` is the description.
- `# TYPE hello_requests_total counter` is the metric type.
- `hello_requests_total{path="/"} 3.0` is the metric name, its labels in braces, and the current value.

The rest of the page has three sources:
- `app.py` defines `hello_requests_total`. It counts visits to `/` and has one label, `path`.
- `observability/red_metrics.py` adds `hello_responses_total` (with `path` and `status`) and the histogram `hello_request_duration_seconds`. Compose loads it next to the unchanged app; Day 44 explains how.
- The Python client adds `process_*` metrics (memory, CPU, open files) and `python_*` metrics for free.

Two details surprise most people. The Python client adds a `_created` series next to each counter, holding the time it was created; you can ignore it. And the names follow conventions from the [naming guide](https://github.com/prometheus/docs/blob/main/docs/practices/naming.md): base units such as seconds and bytes, `_total` at the end of counters, and a prefix for the app.

Prometheus 3 is strict about the HTTP `Content-Type` header of this page. If it is missing or wrong, the scrape fails. Client libraries set it for you.

sections.h: A time series is a name plus labels
sections.body:
This is the most important idea in Prometheus. A time series is identified by its metric name plus the exact set of label values. Change any label value and you have a different series.

The app's page shows `hello_responses_total` three times, with three label sets: `/` and 200, `/healthz` and 200, `/` and 500. That is three time series. Each scrape adds one sample to each: a timestamp and a value.

Prometheus adds two labels of its own when it stores them:
- `job`: the job name from `prometheus.yml`, here `hello-devops`.
- `instance`: the target's address, here `web:8000`.

So the full name of one series in the lab is `hello_responses_total{instance="web:8000", job="hello-devops", path="/", status="500"}`. If you think in databases, the labels are a composite primary key, and each scrape appends a row to every key.

Prometheus also writes a few series per target that the app never showed. `up` is 1 or 0 for each scrape, and `scrape_duration_seconds` tells you how long it took. When a scrape takes longer than `scrape_timeout` (10 seconds by default), it fails with `context deadline exceeded` and `up` becomes 0.

sections.h: Four metric types
sections.body:
Every metric has one of four types. The type tells you which questions it can answer.

A counter only goes up, or drops to zero when the process restarts. `hello_responses_total` and `process_cpu_seconds_total` are counters. The raw value is rarely useful; you ask how fast it grows, which is `rate()` on Day 43.

A gauge is a value that goes up and down: memory in use, queue length, temperature. `process_resident_memory_bytes` for the app read 48,803,840 bytes (about 49 MB) in my run. You read a gauge as it is, and you never take its `rate()`.

A histogram counts observations into buckets. Each bucket has an upper limit, the `le` label (less than or equal), and the buckets are cumulative. In my run the app's `/` route showed `le="0.005"` 759 and `le="0.01"` 1009: 759 requests took 5 ms or less, and 1009 took 10 ms or less. Next to the buckets come `_sum` (all the seconds added up) and `_count` (how many). From these, Prometheus can estimate percentiles and add them up across many servers.

A summary computes percentiles inside the app and shows them with a `quantile` label. Prometheus itself has one: `go_gc_duration_seconds{quantile="0.5"}`. Summaries from several servers cannot be combined, because you cannot average percentiles. That is why the [docs](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/) usually point you to histograms.

Quick rule: counting events, use a counter; measuring a level, a gauge; timing things or sizes, a histogram.

sections.h: Cardinality: why user IDs never go in labels
sections.body:
Labels look free, and this trips most people up. Each new label value creates new series, and series cost memory, disk and query time.

Count the app's histogram. It has one label, `path`, and the default buckets give 15 `le` values. Each path therefore costs 15 bucket series plus `_sum`, `_count` and `_created`, and the counter adds 2 more. In the lab, one request to a new route took the `hello_*` series from 44 to 64.

Now imagine someone adds a `user_id` label so they can see requests per user. With 10,000 users, that is 200,000 series for one route, from one app instance. The [instrumentation guide](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/) suggests keeping most metrics under 10 series and looking hard at anything that could pass 100.

Rules that keep you safe:
- Labels hold small, fixed sets of values: status code, HTTP method, route pattern.
- Never put user IDs, email addresses, request IDs or raw URLs in labels.
- Record the route pattern, not the URL. `red_metrics.py` uses Flask's rule, so `/nope` and `/admin.php` both become `unmatched`.
- Details about single requests belong in logs and traces (Part 11).

For scale: the whole lab, with all four jobs, holds about 2,200 series.

sections.h: Storage, retention and what changed in Prometheus 3
sections.body:
The TSDB keeps recent samples in memory and in a write-ahead log, then writes them to disk in two-hour blocks. Old blocks are merged in the background. By default it keeps 15 days of data (`--storage.tsdb.retention.time`); the lab keeps 7. The [storage docs](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage/) say plainly that local storage is not clustered or replicated. For months of history or a backup, you send data elsewhere, which Day 44 covers.

Prometheus 3.0 came out in November 2024, the first major version in seven years. What you will notice:
- A new web UI. The Query page has Table, Graph and Explain tabs, and Explore metrics in its menu lists every metric name.
- Metric and label names may use any UTF-8 characters, such as dots from OpenTelemetry. Such names need quotes in PromQL.
- An OTLP receiver, turned on with `--web.enable-otlp-receiver`, so OpenTelemetry apps can push metrics in.
- Native histograms, a more precise histogram, are stable since 3.8 but stay off unless you turn them on.
- Some old flags were removed. Tutorials written for Prometheus 2 may show flags that no longer start.

The details are in the [Prometheus 3.0 announcement](https://prometheus.io/blog/2024/11/14/prometheus-3-0/).

lessons.analogy: Prometheus is like a meter reader who walks past every house on a fixed round, every 15 seconds. Each house shows its meters through the window (the /metrics page), and the reader writes down every number with the time and the house address (the labels). If a house does not answer, the reader notes that too, which is up = 0. Where it breaks: a real meter reader cannot be overwhelmed by one house, but an app that invents a new label value per user creates thousands of new meters for Prometheus to read and store.

# The monitoring lab for Parts 9 and 10: hello-devops plus everything that watches it.
#
# Start it from this folder:  docker compose up -d --build
# Then open:
#   http://localhost:8000  hello-devops
#   http://localhost:9090  Prometheus
#   http://localhost:9093  Alertmanager
#   http://localhost:3000  Grafana (user admin, password admin)
# Stop it:                    docker compose down     (add -v to delete the stored data too)
#
# Port 8000 is also used by the Day 15 stack in the repo root. Stop that one first.

services:
  # The app, built from the Dockerfile in the repo root.
  web:
    build: ..
    # One gunicorn worker process: each process keeps its own counters, and with
    # two, every scrape would see a different number (Day 42 explains).
    # Four threads in that process, so one slow request cannot block the
    # /metrics page that Prometheus scrapes.
    # "red_metrics:app" loads red_metrics.py, which adds status and latency
    # metrics to the unchanged app.py (Day 44 explains).
    command:
      - gunicorn
      - --bind=0.0.0.0:8000
      - --workers=1
      - --threads=4
      - --no-control-socket
      - red_metrics:app
    volumes:
      - ./red_metrics.py:/app/red_metrics.py:ro
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  # Scrapes every target, stores the samples, runs the rules.
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.15.1
    command:
      - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - --storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
      - --storage.tsdb.retention.time=7d # keep a week of data (default 15d)
      - --web.enable-lifecycle # allows: curl -X POST localhost:9090/-/reload
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus:/etc/prometheus:ro
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"

  # Machine metrics. On a Mac, containers run inside Docker Desktop's Linux VM,
  # so these numbers describe that VM, not macOS.
  node-exporter:
    image: prom/node-exporter:v1.12.1
    ports:
      - "9100:9100"

  # Receives alerts from Prometheus, groups them and routes them to receivers.
  alertmanager:
    image: prom/alertmanager:v0.34.2
    command:
      - --config.file=/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml
      - --storage.path=/alertmanager
    volumes:
      - ./alertmanager:/etc/alertmanager:ro
      - alertmanager-data:/alertmanager # keeps silences across restarts
    ports:
      - "9093:9093"

  # A stand-in for Slack or PagerDuty: prints each alert it receives.
  # Read it with: docker compose logs -f webhook
  webhook:
    image: python:3.14-slim
    command: ["python", "-u", "/webhook.py"]
    volumes:
      - ./webhook.py:/webhook.py:ro

  # Dashboards (Part 10). The provisioning and dashboards folders come from Day 45.
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:13.3.0
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER: admin
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: admin
    volumes:
      - ./grafana/provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro
      - ./grafana/dashboards:/var/lib/grafana/dashboards:ro
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - prometheus

volumes:
  prometheus-data:
  alertmanager-data:

code.title: observability/red_metrics.py
code.src:
"""Add RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) to hello-devops without editing app.py.

app.py only counts visits to "/" in hello_requests_total. It does not record
status codes or how long a request took. This file imports the unchanged app
and adds two Flask hooks: one runs before every request, one after it.

compose.yaml starts gunicorn with "red_metrics:app" instead of "app:app".
Both metrics land in the same registry, so the app's /metrics page shows them.
"""

import time

from flask import g, request
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram

from app import app  # the hello-devops app, unchanged

# Every response, labelled by route and status code ("200", "404", "500").
RESPONSES = Counter(
    "hello_responses_total",
    "HTTP responses sent, by route and status code",
    ["path", "status"],
)

# How long each request took, in seconds, counted into buckets.
# No buckets given, so the client's defaults apply: 5 ms up to 10 s.
DURATION = Histogram(
    "hello_request_duration_seconds",
    "Time spent handling a request, in seconds",
    ["path"],
)


@app.before_request
def start_timer():
    g.start = time.perf_counter()


@app.after_request
def record(response):
    # Use the route pattern ("/", "/healthz"), never the raw URL.
    # Raw URLs would give one time series per URL anyone ever typed.
    path = request.url_rule.rule if request.url_rule else "unmatched"
    if path != "/metrics":  # do not count Prometheus's own scrapes
        RESPONSES.labels(path=path, status=str(response.status_code)).inc()
        DURATION.labels(path=path).observe(time.perf_counter() - g.start)
    return response

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate in 3 to 4 sentences how a number in app.py ends up stored in Prometheus. Mention the /metrics page, the scrape, labels and what makes one time series different from another.
explain_back.answer: The app keeps counters in memory and prints their current values on its /metrics page in a simple text format. Every 15 seconds Prometheus scrapes that page, adds job and instance labels, and stores one timestamped sample per series. A series is the metric name plus one exact set of label values, so hello_responses_total with status 200 and with status 500 are two series. That is why every new label value costs a new series, and why user IDs never go in labels.

recap: Prometheus pulls: it scrapes each target's /metrics page every scrape interval and records up = 0 when a scrape fails.
One server scrapes, stores samples in its TSDB, runs rules and answers PromQL; exporters give /metrics pages to things that have none.
A time series is a metric name plus one exact set of label values; Prometheus adds job and instance.
Counters only go up, gauges go up and down, histograms count observations into cumulative buckets, summaries cannot be combined.
Every new label value is a new series, so keep labels to small fixed sets and never use user IDs or raw URLs.
Data stays on local disk for 15 days by default; Prometheus 3 brought a new UI, UTF-8 names and an OTLP receiver.

check.q: A metric `orders_total` has labels `country` (40 values) and `payment_method` (5 values), and it runs on 3 instances. At most how many series can it create?
check.why: Series multiply across labels: 40 times 5 times 3 instances is 600.

check.q: You want to track how many jobs are waiting in a queue right now. Which metric type fits?
options: Gauge
Counter
Histogram
Summary
check.why: Queue length goes up and down, which is exactly what a gauge is for.

check.q: A nightly backup script runs for 30 seconds and then exits. Prometheus scrapes every minute. What is the usual way to get its result into Prometheus?
options: Scrape it every second so you catch it
Add a backup_id label to every metric
Push the result to a Pushgateway at the end of the job
Write the result into the app's /metrics page by hand
check.why: A short batch job may finish between scrapes, and recording its outcome is the main case the Pushgateway exists for.

interview.q: Why does Prometheus pull metrics instead of having apps push them?
interview.a: With pull, Prometheus knows the full list of targets, so a target that stops answering shows up at once as up = 0. Pull also keeps the app simple: it only holds counters in memory and serves a page, and a slow monitoring server cannot block it. You can debug by opening the same page with curl. Push is still right for short batch jobs, through the Pushgateway, and Prometheus 3 can also accept OTLP pushes from OpenTelemetry.

interview.q: What is cardinality and why does it matter?
interview.a: Cardinality is the number of time series a metric creates, which is the product of the number of values of each label. Every series costs memory in the server and work for every query that touches it. A label with unbounded values, such as user IDs or raw URLs, can turn one metric into hundreds of thousands of series and slow or crash Prometheus. I keep labels to small fixed sets and put per-request details in logs or traces.

interview.q: When would you choose a histogram over a summary?
interview.a: Almost always, for request latency. A histogram exposes bucket counters, so you can add them up across all instances and then compute a percentile with histogram_quantile. A summary computes percentiles inside each process, and you cannot average percentiles from several processes into a correct total. Summaries can still make sense for one process when you need an exact percentile and never aggregate. The trade-off of a histogram is that its accuracy depends on the bucket limits you choose.

deeper.body:
Why does the lab run gunicorn with one worker process and four threads, when the Dockerfile from Day 16 runs two workers? Because of how counters live in memory.

Gunicorn starts separate worker processes. Each Python process has its own copy of every counter, and each scrape of `/metrics` is answered by whichever worker is free. I started the plain image with two workers, sent 10 requests at once, and then read `/metrics` six times:
- `hello_requests_total{path="/"} 3.0`
- `hello_requests_total{path="/"} 7.0`
- then 3, 3, 3 and 7 again.

Neither number is the truth (10). Worse, Prometheus sees the counter drop from 7 to 3, treats it as a restart, and `rate()` counts the jump as new requests. Your request rate looks higher than it is, and it jumps around.

The [Python client docs](https://github.com/prometheus/client_python/blob/master/docs/content/multiprocess/_index.md) say it directly: client libraries assume a threaded model, where all workers share the metrics. You have three fixes:
- One process per container, with threads for concurrency. The lab does this, and Kubernetes adds more pods when you need more capacity.
- The client's multiprocess mode: every worker writes to files in a shared folder, and `/metrics` adds them up. It has limits, listed in that doc.
- A language whose runtime is one process with many threads, such as the JVM. A Spring Boot app has one set of counters however many requests it serves at once.

The threads matter for a second reason. With one worker and one thread, I froze Redis with `docker compose pause redis`. Every request to `/` then hung for more than 10 seconds while the Redis client waited and retried. The scrape of `/metrics` waited behind them, failed after 10 seconds with `context deadline exceeded`, and `up` went to 0. The app was alive but Prometheus was blind, and the error counters it needed never arrived. With four threads, one thread can answer the scrape while others wait on Redis.

Try the first experiment yourself: `docker run --rm -p 8001:8000 hello-devops:1.0.0` runs the image's own two-worker command. Send a burst of parallel requests with `for i in $(seq 10); do curl -s localhost:8001/ > /dev/null & done`, then read `/metrics` a few times.

guess.q: Prometheus scrapes every 15 seconds. What does rate(hello_responses_total[10s]) return?
options: Requests per second over the last 10 seconds
Zero for every series
An error about the range being too short
Nothing at all: an empty result
guess.why: rate() needs at least two samples inside the range. A 10-second window usually holds only one sample at a 15-second scrape, so the series drops out of the result without any error.

terms.plain: Prometheus's query language: you select series by name and labels, then do maths on them.
A set of series with one value each, all for the same moment.
A set of series with all their samples over a time window, such as the last 5 minutes.
A filter on a label inside braces: = and != for exact values, =~ and !~ for regular expressions.

sections.h: Where to type PromQL, and what comes back
sections.body:
PromQL is the language you use to ask Prometheus questions. You can type it in two places. The web UI at `localhost:9090` has a Query page: the Table tab shows the current value of each series, the Graph tab draws them over time, and the Explain tab breaks a query into parts. In the terminal, the `q` function from Day 42 runs the same query through `promtool`.

The simplest query is a metric name. `hello_responses_total` returned three series in my run, one per label set:
- `{path="/", status="200"} 303`
- `{path="/healthz", status="200"} 3`
- `{path="unmatched", status="404"} 1`

(I left out the `job` and `instance` labels to keep the lines short.) That result is an instant vector: one value per series, all for the same moment. Prometheus takes the newest sample that is at most 5 minutes old. A series nobody has scraped for 5 minutes drops out.

Add a duration in square brackets and you get a range vector: every sample in that window. `hello_responses_total{path="/"}[1m]` returned four samples, 99, 167, 235 and 303, 15 seconds apart. The Graph tab cannot draw a range vector. Functions such as `rate()` take it as input and turn it back into one value per series.

sections.h: Choosing series with label matchers
sections.body:
Braces after the name filter by label. There are four matchers:
- `=` exact: `{path="/"}` keeps only the root route.
- `!=` not equal: `{path!="/"}` returned `/healthz` and `unmatched`.
- `=~` regex: `{status=~"5.."}` means any 5xx status.
- `!~` regex, negated: `{path!~"/|/healthz"}` keeps every other route.

Regexes match the whole value, as if they started with `^` and ended with `$`. So `{path=~"/health"}` returned nothing, while `{path=~"/health.*"}` found `/healthz`. In the shell, wrap the whole query in single quotes so the double quotes inside survive.

An empty result is not zero. It means no series matched, and this trips most people up. Before the app had ever failed, `hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}` returned nothing, because no series with a 5xx label existed yet. Any maths with an empty side is empty too, so an error ratio showed nothing instead of 0. Adding `or vector(0)` to the error part gives a real zero.

sections.h: Counters need rate()
sections.body:
A raw counter only tells you how many requests the process served since it started. It also falls back to zero on every restart: when I recreated the `web` container, the counter went from 2370 to 11.

`rate(hello_responses_total{path="/"}[1m])` gives the average increase per second over the last minute: 4.56 in my run, from a loop sending about 4.5 requests a second. It treats a drop as a restart and adds the new count on top. After that restart, `resets()` counted 1 reset and `rate()` still read 3.3 per second.

Choose the range carefully:
- Use at least 4 times the scrape interval. With a 15-second scrape, `[10s]` returned nothing and `[1m]` worked.
- Longer ranges are smoother but slower to react. Dashboards often use `[5m]`.
- Right after a start, long ranges read low. At two minutes old, `[5m]` gave 1.55 while `[1m]` gave 4.44. Five minutes later they agreed: 4.49 and 4.56.

Two relatives:
- `increase(x[1m])` is the rate times 60: "how many in the last minute". It returned 266.67, not a whole number, because it estimates to the edges of the window. Once it even said 1216.6 for a counter that read 1175.
- `irate(x[1m])` uses only the last two samples. It is jumpy, fine for a zoomed-in graph and wrong for alerts.

How exactly does PromQL calculate rates? (PromLabs)

sections.h: Aggregation: sum, by and without
sections.body:
`rate()` returns one result per series. Usually you want fewer lines. `sum(rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))` added everything into one number: 3.53 requests a second.

Add `by` to keep some labels, or `without` to drop some:
- `sum by (path) (rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))` gave `/` 3.51, `/healthz` 0.028 and `unmatched` 0.
- `sum without (instance, status) (...)` drops only those two labels and keeps `job` and `path`.

The `/healthz` line is the Docker health check from Day 16: one request every 30 seconds is about 0.03 a second. Aggregation shows you traffic you did not know about.

Other aggregations work the same way:
- `avg`, `min` and `max`, such as `max by (job) (process_resident_memory_bytes)`.
- `count`, such as `count by (job) (up)` for the number of targets per job.
- `topk(2, ...)` and `bottomk`, for the largest or smallest few series.

Always take the rate first, then sum. Each instance's counter restarts on its own, and only `rate()` can see that, one series at a time. Robust Perception's post [Rate then sum](https://www.robustperception.io/rate-then-sum-never-sum-then-rate/) shows what goes wrong otherwise.

refs.title: Rate then sum, never sum then rate (Robust Perception)

sections.h: Maths between series: ratios, filters and matching
sections.body:
You can divide one query by another. The error ratio is failed responses per second divided by all responses per second: `sum(rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))`.

Between two vectors, Prometheus pairs series whose labels are exactly the same. For a per-path error ratio I wrote `sum by (path, status) (...)` on the left and `sum by (path) (...)` on the right, and got nothing: the left side has a `status` label the right side lacks. Adding `/ ignoring(status)` between them, or `/ on(path)`, gave `/` 0.054 and `/readyz` NaN. NaN is 0 divided by 0: nobody called `/readyz` in that window.

Comparison operators filter:
- `job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate5m > 0.02` keeps series above 2% and drops the rest. Alert rules use this form.
- `... > bool 0.02` returns 1 or 0 for every series instead.

Three more tools:
- `offset` looks back in time. `hello_responses_total{path="/"} offset 5m` read 30 while the live value was 1380.
- `up == 0` lists every target whose last scrape failed.
- `absent(up{job="payments"})` returns 1 when no such series exists at all. It catches a job that vanished, which `up == 0` cannot.

sections.h: Latency from histograms
sections.body:
Each histogram bucket is a counter, so you treat it like one. Take the rate of every bucket, add them up while keeping `le`, then let `histogram_quantile()` estimate the percentile:
`histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(hello_request_duration_seconds_bucket{path="/"}[5m])))`

In my healthy run that gave a p95 of 0.018 seconds, a p50 of 0.0036 and a p99 of 0.045. The average comes from the other two series: `rate(..._sum[5m]) / rate(..._count[5m])` gave 0.0060. Drop `le` from the `by` clause and the result is empty, because the function needs the bucket limits.

The answer is an estimate. The function finds the bucket that holds the 95th percentile and assumes requests are spread evenly inside it. Two real examples:
- Prometheus's own query API answered in a few milliseconds, but its first bucket is 0 to 0.1 seconds. The p95 came out at exactly 0.095.
- During a Redis outage, hello-devops's p95 read 6.12 seconds: somewhere in the 5 to 7.5 second bucket.

If most requests are slower than the largest finite bucket, the function can only return that bucket's limit, 10 seconds for the default buckets. So choose bucket limits around the latencies you care about. And never average percentiles from several servers. Sum the buckets, then compute the percentile once, as the [histograms guide](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/) explains.

sections.h: RED for hello-devops, saved as recording rules
sections.body:
Put the pieces together and you have RED for hello-devops, per job:
- Rate: `sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))`
- Errors: `sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))`
- Duration: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (job, le) (rate(hello_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))`

Dashboards and alerts will run these every few seconds, forever. A recording rule runs a query on Prometheus's schedule (every 15 seconds in the lab) and stores the answer as a new series. Reading that series is cheap, and every dashboard and alert gets the same number.

The lab keeps them in `observability/prometheus/rules/recording.yml`. The names follow the [naming convention](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/rules/) `level:metric:operations`, for example `job:hello_responses:rate5m`: grouped by job, from `hello_responses`, a 5-minute rate. `prometheus.yml` loads every file in `rules/`. After an edit, check the file with `promtool`, reload Prometheus, and query the new name. Status, Rule health in the UI shows each rule and its last error.

code.title: observability/prometheus/rules/recording.yml
code.src:
# Recording rules (Day 43): Prometheus runs each expr every 15 seconds and
# stores the result as a new series named after "record".
# Names follow level:metric:operations, for example job:hello_responses:rate5m.
groups:
  - name: hello-devops-recording
    rules:
      # Rate: requests per second, per job.
      - record: job:hello_responses:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))

      # Errors: the share of responses with a 5xx status, over five windows.
      # The SLO alerts in alerts.yml compare a long and a short window.
      - record: job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[5m]))
      - record: job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate30m
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[30m]))
          /
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[30m]))
      - record: job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[1h]))
          /
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[1h]))
      - record: job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate6h
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[6h]))
          /
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[6h]))
      - record: job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate3d
        expr: |
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[3d]))
          /
          sum by (job) (rate(hello_responses_total[3d]))

      # Duration: the 95th percentile latency in seconds, per job.
      - record: job:hello_request_duration_seconds:p95_5m
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (job, le) (rate(hello_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

interview.q: What is the difference between rate(), irate() and increase()?
interview.a: rate() gives the average per-second increase of a counter over the whole range and handles counter resets, so it is the default for graphs and alerts. irate() uses only the last two samples in the range, which reacts fast but is noisy, so it suits zoomed-in graphs of busy counters and not alerts. increase() is rate() multiplied by the range in seconds, so it reads as a count, but because of extrapolation it can return fractions. All three need at least two samples in the range.

interview.q: How do you compute a p95 latency in Prometheus, and what are the pitfalls?
interview.a: You take rate() of the histogram's _bucket series, sum them by le (plus any labels you want to keep), and pass that to histogram_quantile(0.95, ...). Pitfalls: dropping le from the sum gives an empty result, averaging percentiles from summaries is mathematically wrong, and the answer is an interpolation inside one bucket. If the buckets are coarse, the p95 can be far from the truth, and if requests are slower than the largest finite bucket you only get that bucket's limit.

A recording rule evaluates an expensive query on a fixed schedule and stores the result as a new series. Dashboards and alerts then read that series cheaply, and everyone uses exactly the same definition, for example of the error ratio. They are also needed for long windows, such as 6-hour or 3-day ratios for SLO alerts, which would be slow to compute on every evaluation from raw data. The convention is to name them level:metric:operations, such as job:http_requests:rate5m.

deeper.body:
Why did `increase()` return 266.67 requests in a minute instead of a whole number? Because `rate()` and `increase()` estimate what happened at the edges of the window.

Inside a one-minute window at a 15-second scrape there are about four samples, for example 99, 167, 235 and 303. The first one is a few seconds after the window starts and the last one a few seconds before it ends. The samples only cover about 45 seconds of the 60. So Prometheus takes the growth it can see (204) and extends the line to both edges of the window, as long as each gap is no more than 1.1 times the usual spacing between samples. The result is 204 scaled up to the full minute, roughly 266. PromLabs' post [How exactly does PromQL calculate rates?](https://promlabs.com/blog/2021/01/29/how-exactly-does-promql-calculate-rates/) walks through the exact rules.

This explains two other numbers from this lesson.
- A five-minute increase once said 1216.6 for a counter that read 1175. The counter was younger than the window, and the estimate added a little at each end.
- A two-minute-old series showed a 5-minute rate of 1.55 while the 1-minute rate was 4.44. When the gap to the window's start is larger than that, Prometheus decides the series began inside the window and stretches the line only half a scrape interval. Then it divides about two minutes of growth by five minutes of time.

It also explains a trap from the task. A counter series that appears for the first time with the value 6 has no earlier sample. `rate()` cannot know whether those 6 happened just now or an hour ago, so it ignores them. Only increases between two scrapes count. That is why well-written apps create their error series at 0 when they start, before any error happens. In Python you call `.labels(...)` once at startup for the label values you expect.

None of this matters much for dashboards and alerts over 5 minutes or more. It matters when you compare Prometheus with exact counts from logs, or alert on increase() of something rare. There, reach for longer windows, and remember the result is an estimate.

lessons.title: Alerting and Prometheus on Kubernetes
lessons.goal: By the end you can write and unit-test alerting rules, route alerts through Alertmanager to a receiver, read how an app records a histogram, and monitor hello-devops on Kubernetes with a ServiceMonitor and a PrometheusRule.

guess.q: An alerting rule has for: 10m. Its condition is true for 8 minutes, false for one evaluation, then true again. When does it fire?
options: At the 10-minute mark, counted from the first time it became true
Right away, because it was already true for 8 minutes
Never, because one false evaluation cancels the rule
10 minutes after the condition became true again
guess.why: One false evaluation sends the alert back to inactive. The pending wait starts again from zero, which is what makes for: a filter against flapping.

terms.plain: A PromQL condition with a name; every series it returns becomes an alert.

Where Alertmanager sends notifications: a webhook, Slack, PagerDuty, email and others.

sections.h: Alerting rules: expr, for, labels, annotations
sections.body:
An alerting rule is a PromQL query with a name. Prometheus runs it every evaluation interval (15 seconds in the lab), and every series the query returns is one active alert. Here is `HelloDown` from `alerts.yml`:
- `expr: up{job="hello-devops"} == 0` is the condition. The comparison filters, so the query returns something only when a scrape fails.
- `for: 1m` means the condition must stay true for a whole minute. Until then the alert is pending.
- `labels: severity: page` is added to the alert. Alertmanager routes on it.
- `annotations` hold text for humans. `{{ $labels.instance }}` and `{{ $value }}` fill in the details.

An alert moves through three states: inactive, pending, firing. If the condition is false for even one evaluation, the alert goes back to inactive and the wait starts again. So `for:` filters out blips such as one slow scrape during a deploy. Prometheus also writes every active alert as a series named `ALERTS`, so `ALERTS{alertstate="pending"}` is a normal query.

The two SLO alerts turn the Day 41 plan into rules. They compare recording rules from Day 43 with the burn-rate lines: page at 14.4 times the budget over 1 hour and 5 minutes, or 6 times over 6 hours and 30 minutes; open a ticket at 1 times over 3 days and 6 hours.

Prometheus only decides that an alert fires. It sends firing alerts to the Alertmanager listed under `alerting:` in `prometheus.yml`, and it does not send any message itself.

sections.h: Alertmanager: routes, groups, inhibition and silences
sections.body:
Alertmanager is a separate service. Its job is to turn a stream of alerts into a few useful messages. It does four things:
- Grouping: alerts with the same `group_by` labels become one notification. Fifty pods failing at once give one message, not fifty.
- Routing: each group walks down a tree of routes, matched on labels, to a receiver. In the lab, `severity="page"` goes to `pager` and everything else to `tickets`.
- Inhibition: while one alert fires, it mutes others. The lab mutes ticket alerts for a job while a page fires for the same job.
- Silences: temporary mutes you create at run time, in the UI on port 9093 or with `amtool`. They are not in the config file.

Three timers control the pace, and the lab shortens all of them:
- `group_wait` (default 30s): wait for more alerts before the first message of a new group.
- `group_interval` (default 5m): wait before telling you about changes to a group already sent.
- `repeat_interval` (default 4h): resend an alert that is still firing.

A receiver is the destination. Alertmanager has built-in support for Slack, PagerDuty, email, Microsoft Teams and more, plus a generic webhook. The lab's `webhook.py` is a 30-line Python server that prints what it receives, so you can see exactly what Slack would get. `send_resolved: true` also sends a message when the alert stops.

sections.h: Test alerts before they page anyone
sections.body:
An alert you never saw fire is a guess. `promtool test rules` lets you prove a rule does what you think, without waiting for a real outage. A test file lists:
1. The rule files to load.
2. Made-up input series. `0+300x90` means start at 0 and add 300 every interval, 90 times.
3. A time to check, and the exact alerts expected then, with labels and annotations.

The lab's `tests/alerts_test.yml` checks three stories: the app is down for two minutes and `HelloDown` fires; errors start at minute 61 and the fast burn pages by minute 75; and a slow leak of 0.33% errors opens a ticket but does not page. When I first wrote the second test I guessed the summary would say 4.115%. promtool printed the expected and the actual alert side by side, `4.762%`, and the fix took ten seconds.

Test the routing tree too: `amtool config routes test severity=page alertname=HelloDown` prints `pager`.

Before you merge a new alert, ask these questions:
- Does it fire on a symptom users feel?
- Does it have a `for:` long enough to skip blips?
- Does it use `rate()`, never `irate()`, so one quiet scrape does not reset it?
- Does the annotation say what is wrong, and link to a runbook?
- Would the person paged know what to do next?

sections.h: Instrumenting an app: counters and histograms in code
sections.body:
Instrumenting means adding metrics to your own code with a client library. Python's is `prometheus_client`; the JVM has Micrometer, which Spring Boot's Actuator uses to record every request as `http.server.requests` and serve it at `/actuator/prometheus`.

hello-devops started with one line: `Counter("hello_requests_total", ...)` and `.labels(path="/").inc()` in the handler. It counts visits, but it cannot see status codes or time. The lab adds both in `observability/red_metrics.py`, without touching `app.py`:
1. It imports the Flask app and registers two hooks: one runs before every request and notes the start time, one runs after it.
2. The after-hook increments `hello_responses_total` with the route and status code.
3. It calls `observe()` on the histogram `hello_request_duration_seconds` with the elapsed seconds. No buckets are given, so the client's defaults apply: 5 ms up to 10 s.
4. It uses Flask's route pattern as the `path` label, so a scan of random URLs adds only one `unmatched` value.

Both metrics land in the client's default registry, which the app's existing `/metrics` route already prints. Compose mounts the file into the container and starts gunicorn with `red_metrics:app`.

Two choices matter more than the code. First, buckets: put limits near the latencies you care about, such as your SLO threshold, because Day 43 showed that `histogram_quantile` can only be as precise as the buckets. Second, the process model: one process per container, with threads, so every scrape sees every request (Day 42).

sections.h: Prometheus on Kubernetes: the Operator and kube-prometheus-stack
sections.body:
On Kubernetes you rarely write `prometheus.yml` by hand. The usual install is the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart (Day 37 covered Helm). With the lab's `values.yaml`, version 92.16.0 rendered 109 objects. The main parts:
- The Prometheus Operator, a controller that runs Prometheus and Alertmanager for you.
- Prometheus and Alertmanager, described as custom resources and run as StatefulSets.
- Grafana with ready-made dashboards for the cluster (Part 10).
- node_exporter as a DaemonSet, one pod per node.
- kube-state-metrics, which turns Kubernetes objects into metrics.
- 134 ready-made alerting rules, such as `KubePodCrashLooping`.

The Operator adds custom resources (Day 30 showed how controllers work):
- `ServiceMonitor` and `PodMonitor`: what to scrape, found by labels.
- `PrometheusRule`: recording and alerting rules.
- `Probe` and `ScrapeConfig`: black-box checks and targets outside the cluster.
- `AlertmanagerConfig`: routes and receivers, per namespace.

Two defaults surprise people. One alert, `Watchdog`, always fires on purpose: if it ever stops arriving, your alerting pipeline is broken. And the chart's default Alertmanager config sends everything to a receiver named `null`, so nobody is notified until you add a real receiver.

sections.h: ServiceMonitors, PrometheusRules and the release label
sections.body:
`observability/servicemonitor.yaml` says: in namespace `hello`, find Services labelled `app: hello-devops`, and scrape their port named `http` at `/metrics` every 15 seconds. The Operator turns that into scrape settings. Prometheus then scrapes each pod behind the Service directly, one target per pod. In Target health they appear under `serviceMonitor/hello/hello-devops/0`.

The labels are richer than in Compose. `job` becomes the Service name, `hello-devops`, and the Operator adds `namespace`, `pod` and `service`. So the same PromQL works in both places, and `sum by (pod)` splits by pod.

This is the gotcha. The chart's Prometheus only reads ServiceMonitors, PodMonitors and PrometheusRules that carry the label `release` with the Helm release name. The lab installs the release as `monitoring`, so both files have `release: monitoring`. Leave it out and nothing fails: no error, no event, and your app never shows up. If a target is missing, check in this order:
1. The `release` label on the ServiceMonitor.
2. Its selector against `kubectl -n hello get svc --show-labels`.
3. The port name: it must match a named port on the Service.

The pods in Kubernetes run the image's own command: two gunicorn workers and no `red_metrics.py`. So `prometheusrule.yaml` alerts only on `up`, which the worker problem from Day 42 cannot confuse. `HelloNoPodsUp` uses `absent()`, because a deleted pod leaves the target list instead of reporting `up = 0`.

sections.h: kube-state-metrics, metrics-server and keeping data longer
sections.body:
Two components sound alike and do different jobs:
- [kube-state-metrics](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-state-metrics) reads the Kubernetes API and exposes the state of objects as metrics: desired and available replicas, pod restarts, job results. Prometheus scrapes it.
- [metrics-server](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server) collects current CPU and memory from each kubelet for `kubectl top` and the autoscaler from Day 35. Its README says it is meant only for autoscaling, not as a source for monitoring.

Then there is time. One Prometheus keeps its data on local disk, 15 days by default, and the docs say that storage is not clustered or replicated. Teams that need months of history, high availability or one view across many clusters add a second layer:
- `remote_write` streams every sample to another system as it arrives.
- [Thanos](https://github.com/thanos-io/thanos) runs next to existing Prometheus servers and keeps their blocks in object storage, such as S3.
- [Grafana Mimir](https://github.com/grafana/mimir) receives remote write into a scalable, multi-tenant store, also backed by object storage.
- Hosted services, such as Grafana Cloud, accept remote write too.

For one laptop cluster, 15 days of local data is plenty. The question to ask at work is how far back an incident review needs to look, and whether losing one Prometheus disk would hurt.

lessons.analogy: Prometheus is a smoke detector and Alertmanager is the building's alarm desk. A detector only decides that there is smoke, and only after it lasts a few seconds (for:). The desk turns ten detectors on one floor into one call (grouping), sends a fire to the fire brigade and a faulty sensor to the caretaker (routing), ignores floor alarms while the whole building is already evacuating (inhibition), and stays quiet during a planned fire drill (a silence). Where it breaks: a real alarm desk is staffed by people, while Alertmanager follows its rules exactly, so a wrong route sends the page nowhere.

code.title: observability/prometheus/rules/alerts.yml
code.src:
# Alerting rules (Day 44). Test them:
#   docker compose exec prometheus promtool test rules /etc/prometheus/tests/alerts_test.yml
#
# The SLO from Day 41: 99.9% of hello-devops responses are not 5xx, over 30 days.
# Error budget = 0.1% (0.001). The burn rates follow Google's SRE Workbook:
#   page:   14.4 over 1 hour (2% of the budget) or 6 over 6 hours (5%)
#   ticket: 1 over 3 days (10%)
# Each long window is paired with a short one (1/12 as long), so an alert
# stops firing a few minutes after the errors stop.
# The lab uses a short "for" so you can watch alerts fire within minutes.
groups:
  - name: hello-devops-alerts
    rules:
      # Symptom: Prometheus cannot reach the app at all.
      - alert: HelloDown
        expr: up{job="hello-devops"} == 0
        for: 1m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "hello-devops at {{ $labels.instance }} is down"
          description: "Prometheus has not been able to scrape {{ $labels.instance }} for 1 minute."

      # Symptom: users get errors fast enough to empty the budget in days.
      - alert: HelloErrorBudgetFastBurn
        expr: |
          (
            job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate1h{job="hello-devops"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
            and
            job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate5m{job="hello-devops"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
          )
          or
          (
            job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate6h{job="hello-devops"} > (6 * 0.001)
            and
            job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate30m{job="hello-devops"} > (6 * 0.001)
          )
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of hello-devops requests fail (fast burn)"
          description: "At this rate the 30-day error budget is gone in less than a week."

      # Symptom: a slow leak. Worth a ticket for working hours, not a page.
      - alert: HelloErrorBudgetSlowBurn
        expr: |
          job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate3d{job="hello-devops"} > 0.001
          and
          job:hello_responses_errors:ratio_rate6h{job="hello-devops"} > 0.001
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: ticket
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of hello-devops requests fail (slow burn)"
          description: "At this rate the 30-day error budget runs out before the month ends."

code.title: observability/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml
code.src:
# Alertmanager settings for the monitoring lab (Day 44).
# Check this file:  docker compose exec alertmanager amtool check-config /etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml

# The routing tree: every alert enters at the top "route" and walks down.
route:
  receiver: tickets # default: anything no child route matches goes here
  group_by: ["alertname", "job"] # one notification per alert name and job
  group_wait: 10s # wait for more alerts of a new group before the first send (default 30s)
  group_interval: 1m # wait before sending changes to a group already sent (default 5m)
  repeat_interval: 1h # resend an alert that is still firing (default 4h)
  routes:
    - matchers: ['severity="page"']
      receiver: pager

# Where notifications go. In real life: PagerDuty, Slack, email, ...
# Here both go to the small webhook service, which prints them.
receivers:
  - name: pager
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://webhook:5001/pager
        send_resolved: true # also tell us when the alert stops
  - name: tickets
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://webhook:5001/tickets
        send_resolved: true

# While a page fires for a job, mute ticket alerts for the same job.
# The page already gets a human's attention, so the ticket is noise.
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: ['severity="page"']
    target_matchers: ['severity="ticket"']
    equal: ["job"]

code.title: observability/webhook.py
code.src:
"""A tiny stand-in for Slack or PagerDuty: print every alert Alertmanager sends.

Alertmanager POSTs JSON to http://webhook:5001/<receiver>. Watch the output with:
    docker compose logs -f webhook
It uses only the Python standard library, so there is nothing to install.
"""

import json
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer


class AlertHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        size = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
        payload = json.loads(self.rfile.read(size))
        # One POST can carry several alerts: Alertmanager groups them.
        for alert in payload["alerts"]:
            labels = alert["labels"]
            print(
                f"[{payload['receiver']}] {alert['status'].upper()} "
                f"{labels['alertname']} job={labels.get('job', '-')} "
                f"severity={labels.get('severity', '-')}: "
                f"{alert['annotations'].get('summary', '')}",
                flush=True,
            )
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass  # skip the default access-log line for every POST


print("webhook: waiting for alerts on port 5001", flush=True)
HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 5001), AlertHandler).serve_forever()
code.run: docker compose up -d alertmanager webhook && docker compose logs -f webhook

code.src:
# Tells Prometheus to scrape hello-devops every 15 seconds (Day 44).
# Needs kube-prometheus-stack (see values.yaml). It finds the Service in
# k8s/service.yaml by its label app: hello-devops and its port named http.
# Apply: kubectl apply -f observability/servicemonitor.yaml
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    # Prometheus from the "monitoring" Helm release only reads
    # ServiceMonitors with this label. Without it, nothing fails:
    # your app just never shows up.
    release: monitoring
spec:
  # Find Services with this label ...
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops
  # ... in this namespace.
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
      - hello
  endpoints:
    # Prometheus finds the pods behind the Service and scrapes each pod
    # directly on the matching container port (8000): one target per pod.
    # The job label becomes the Service name: job="hello-devops".
    - port: http # the NAME of the Service port, not its number
      path: /metrics
      interval: 15s

code.title: observability/prometheusrule.yaml
code.src:
# Alerting rules for hello-devops on Kubernetes (Day 44).
# Needs kube-prometheus-stack (see values.yaml). The Prometheus Operator
# turns this object into a rule file and loads it into Prometheus.
# Apply: kubectl apply -f observability/prometheusrule.yaml
#
# On Kubernetes the pods run the image's default command: two gunicorn
# workers and no red_metrics.py. So these rules use only "up", which
# Prometheus records for every scrape and which no worker can confuse.
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    # Like ServiceMonitors, rules are only read when they carry the
    # release label of the "monitoring" Helm release.
    release: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
    - name: hello-devops
      rules:
        # No pod answers its scrape. A dead pod leaves the target list,
        # so "up == 0" alone would miss this case; absent() catches it.
        - alert: HelloNoPodsUp
          expr: absent(up{job="hello-devops", namespace="hello"} == 1)
          for: 2m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "No hello-devops pod in namespace hello can be scraped"

        # One pod is still listed but does not answer its scrape.
        - alert: HelloPodNotScraped
          expr: up{job="hello-devops", namespace="hello"} == 0
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Pod {{ $labels.pod }} has not answered a scrape for 5 minutes"
